statement: In a class, the mean test score of the boys is 66 and the mean score of the girls is 76. The mean score of the whole class is 72. What fraction of the class are girls?

choices.misconception: I matched the gaps the wrong way round, giving the girls the share of their own gap, 4 out of 10.
I assumed there are equally many boys and girls without checking it against the class mean.
I took the ratio of the two gaps, 4 to 6, and wrote it as the fraction 4/6 of the class.
I found the ratio of girls to boys, 6 to 4, and gave it instead of the fraction of the class.

hints: Is the class mean nearer to the boys' mean or to the girls' mean?
A combined mean is a weighted average, so it sits closer to the larger group. Compare the distances from the class mean to each group's mean; the group sizes are in the opposite ratio.
The class mean is 6 above the boys' mean and 4 below the girls' mean.

solutions.reliable: Let g be the fraction of the class who are girls. Then 76g + 66(1 - g) = 72, so 66 + 10g = 72 and g = 6/10 = 3/5. The transferable idea: a weighted average sits closer to the heavier group, with the weights in inverse ratio to the distances.
solutions.elegant: The distances are 6 from the boys' mean and 4 from the girls' mean, so girls : boys = 6 : 4 = 3 : 2, and the girls make up 3/5 of the class.

whyOnTest: The class mean leans toward the bigger group; reading the gaps the right way round is the whole problem, and both wrong readings are offered.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
